newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Ireland launches jobs program before election.
newsitem.headline: Ireland launches jobs program before election.

text.p: The Irish government, widely expected to call an election this week and trailing opposition parties in the opinion polls, on Tuesday unveiled a programme pledging to halve unemployment in the next 10 years.

"This will provide the soundest platform for future jobs growth and social cohesion into the next century. We want to halve unemployment, including long-term unemployment," Richard Bruton, minister for enterprise and employment said in a statement.

The centrepiece of the programme is a pledge to slash corporation taxes to a standard rate of 12.5 percent by the year 2011 in a bid to sustain the country's economic and employment boom and woo more foreign investment.
Top rates are as high as 36 percent at present although manufacturing companies currently enjoy a 10 percent rate.
Unemployment has been falling steadily in Ireland. The number of people claiming unemployment benefit in April dropped to a seasonally-adjusted 256,000 from 260,000 a month earlier.
Bruton said his government had generated 150,000 new jobs over the last three years.
Prime Minister John Bruton said in a separate statement the government was committed to full employment "over time' as the central goal of its jobs policy.

Irish media reports said the programme, entitled "Growing our Employment -- Sharing our Growth," was aiming to propel Ireland into the top 10 most competitive economies in the world. Another plank of the programme is a new 25 percent tax rate on passive income, such as rent from property.
